opus-5.5.text:
I think school, including MIT, is actually a pretty good place to learn how to handle conflict, because the stakes feel high to you at the time but they're relatively low in the bigger picture. You're working on problem sets with friends, doing group projects, sharing labs, competing a little for attention or recognition. Friction is natural in all of that.

What I've noticed is that the most common way people handle conflict is to avoid it. Engineers especially, myself included, would rather go back to the code than have an uncomfortable conversation. If a teammate isn't pulling their weight, or two people disagree about a technical direction, people often just stay quiet, do the work themselves, and let resentment build. That feels efficient in the short term, but it rarely is.

At MIT the conflicts are often about ideas, which is actually healthy. People argue hard about which approach is right, which design is cleaner, which result is real. The best version of that is when everyone separates the idea from the person. You can say, "I think this approach is wrong, and here's why," and nobody takes it personally. The worst version is when ego gets attached and the discussion becomes about who's smarter rather than what's true.

What I learned over time is that being direct but respectful is usually the fastest path. Say the thing early, be specific, assume good intentions, and focus on the shared goal. Most people actually appreciate it. And if you can't resolve something, it's okay to step back, sleep on it, and come back with a clearer head. Later, when I started building a team and a company, I realized those small lessons from school mattered a lot. Technical problems are hard, but people problems are often harder. And learning to handle them calmly is one of the most valuable things you can take away from university.

r001.rationale: The response says that people commonly avoid conflict in school, explicitly including engineers at MIT who stay quiet rather than address disagreements.

fable-5.1.text:
That's an interesting question, because I think the way conflict gets handled in school really depends on the culture of the place, and MIT was quite different from what I grew up with.

Back in China, at least when I was a student, conflict was often something you avoided. If you disagreed with a professor or a senior student, you usually didn't say it directly. There was a lot of emphasis on harmony and respecting hierarchy, so disagreements kind of got buried, and people would just quietly do their own thing. That has some advantages, but it also means a lot of problems never actually get resolved.

At MIT, what struck me was how direct people were, especially in research. In group meetings, people would challenge each other's ideas openly, even students challenging faculty. At first that felt a bit uncomfortable to me, honestly. But over time I realized it was mostly not personal. The conflict was about the idea, not about the person. People could argue intensely about whether an approach made sense, and then go get lunch together afterward. I came to really appreciate that, because it's how you get to the truth faster.

That said, I don't want to romanticize it. Not everyone handles it well. Some people are direct in a way that's actually just harsh, and students who come from more reserved cultures can feel steamrolled in those settings. I saw international students, including myself early on, stay quiet in discussions not because they had nothing to say, but because the style of argument felt foreign. So I think the healthiest environments I experienced were ones where advisors were deliberate about that, where they'd explicitly ask for dissenting opinions and make it safe to disagree.

If I had to summarize, I'd say good conflict in school is when it's focused on the problem, everyone feels they can participate, and it ends with people learning something. Bad conflict is when it's about ego or status. And I think a lot of what I learned about running a team later, with Taichi and the startup, came from watching which of those two modes was happening in the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says conflict was often avoided in China, but describes MIT as direct and open to disagreement, so it does not say school culture tends to avoid conflict even at MIT.

astra-6.text:
I think school gives you a fairly structured environment for handling disagreement. If we disagree about a math problem, we can work through it and see which answer is correct. But when the disagreement is about priorities, or how people want to work together, there may not be one right answer.

Even at MIT, being very good at solving technical problems doesn’t automatically make someone good at handling those situations. You still need to listen and understand what the other person cares about. I think the important thing is to be comfortable disagreeing without turning it into a personal conflict. You can question someone’s idea and still respect them.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses structured disagreement at school and conflict handling at MIT, but does not say that school culture tends to avoid conflict.

sol-6.1.text: I think in school, including at MIT, people often approach conflict as if it were a problem with a correct answer. You explain your reasoning, I explain mine, and hopefully we figure out who is right. That works well for some technical disagreements. But when the conflict involves feelings, expectations, or different priorities, being right doesn’t necessarily resolve it. You also have to listen and understand why the other person sees things differently.

r001.rationale: The response describes how people approach conflict when it occurs, but does not say that school culture tends to avoid conflict, including at MIT.
